recent_posts.title: Playground in Prod - Optimising Agents in Production Environments — Samuel Colvin, Pydantic
recent_posts.summary: Samuel Colvin, creator of Pydantic, presents a workshop on optimizing AI agents in production using two tools: Jepper (a genetic/Pareto-based prompt optimization library) and Pydantic Logfire's managed variables feature. The demo uses a real-world task of identifying political dynasties among UK MPs by analyzing Wikipedia pages with a Pydantic AI agent. He walks through running evals against a golden dataset, comparing a basic vs. expert-written prompt (87% vs. 92% accuracy), then using Jepper to automatically optimize the prompt to ~96.7% accuracy. The second half covers Logfire managed variables, which allow changing agent configuration (instructions, model, temperature) in production without redeployment, using an OpenFeature-compatible AB testing mechanism. Key discussion points include overfitting risks, the value of optimization for private/domain-specific data, fine-tuning vs. prompt optimization tradeoffs, and the challenge of defining good eval metrics.

recent_posts.title: Vibe Engineering Effect Apps — Michael Arnaldi, Effectful
recent_posts.summary: A live workshop demonstrating 'vibe engineering' — building a TypeScript HTTP API from scratch using AI coding agents (OpenCode with GPT) and the Effect library, without writing code by hand. The core technique: clone the Effect repository directly into your project so AI agents can learn from the source code rather than relying on outdated training data or MCP documentation servers. The session covers setting up a Bun/Vitest project, configuring strict TypeScript diagnostics to act as AI feedback loops, generating pattern markdown files from library source code, building a todo REST API with OpenAPI docs and SQLite persistence via Effect SQL, and writing ESLint rules to prevent common AI-generated anti-patterns. Key insights include keeping context windows small and focused, using spec-driven development with persisted markdown plans, and treating repository setup as the primary job of a developer in an AI-assisted workflow.

recent_posts.title: How to monitor AI agents in production using observability signals
recent_posts.summary: A talk and workshop on agent observability, covering why traditional eval-based testing is insufficient for production AI agents. Key topics include implicit signals (classifiers for user frustration, refusals, task failure) vs explicit signals (error rates, latency, cost), using regex patterns as cheap monitoring signals, self-diagnostics via a report tool that encourages agents to surface their own anomalous behavior, and A/B experimentation using semantic signals to measure the impact of prompt or model changes. The Raindrop platform is demonstrated as a production monitoring tool that provides trajectory visualization, alerting, clustering of user intents, and a triage agent that automatically investigates signal spikes.

recent_posts.title: Skills at Scale — Nick Nisi and Zack Proser, WorkOS
recent_posts.summary: Workshop transcript from WorkOS developer experience engineers Nick Nisi and Zack Proser covering 'skills' — reusable, composable markdown-based instruction units for AI coding agents like Claude. Skills solve the problem of repeatedly re-injecting context into stateless LLM conversations. Key topics include: skill structure (YAML front matter with name/description for LLM routing, optional scripts for deterministic data injection), when to use skills vs. claude.md memory files, progressive disclosure to avoid bloating context windows, confidence scoring patterns, skill evaluation frameworks, team-scale skill sharing and governance challenges, and skill marketplaces. The workshop includes a hands-on 'repo roast' skill-building exercise and Q&A covering skill conflicts, sub-agents vs. skills, and organizational management of shared skill libraries.

recent_posts.title: Multi-Agent Systems That Ship for Days — Luke Alvoeiro, Factory
recent_posts.summary: Luke Alvoeiro from Factory presents a multi-agent architecture called 'Missions' designed to run software development tasks autonomously for days or weeks. The core argument is that the bottleneck in modern software engineering is human attention, not intelligence. Missions uses a three-role architecture: orchestrators (planning), workers (implementation), and validators (verification). Key design decisions include serial feature execution to avoid agent conflicts, validation contracts written before any code to define correctness independently of implementation, structured handoffs between agents to preserve context, and model-agnostic design so the right LLM can be placed in each role. The system combines five multi-agent communication patterns: delegation, creator-verifier, broadcast, negotiation, and direct communication. Production results show missions running up to 16 days, with 50% of final code being tests and 90% test coverage. The architecture is prompt-driven rather than hard-coded to improve automatically as models improve.

recent_posts.title: MCP UI: Extending the frontier — Liad Yosef and Ido Salomon, MCP Apps
recent_posts.summary: MCP Apps is an official extension to the MCP (Model Context Protocol) standard, co-created with Anthropic and OpenAI, that enables MCP servers to return rich, interactive UI components instead of plain text responses. Tools like ChatGPT, Claude, VS Code, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot have already adopted it. The spec standardizes bidirectional communication between embedded UI chunks and the host, allowing user interactions (clicks, form inputs) to trigger tool calls or prompts back to the model. The talk covers the architecture, a spectrum of UI generation approaches (predefined, declarative, fully generative), upcoming features like reusable views and model-driven UI interaction, and positions MCP Apps as a new application distribution paradigm rivaling the App Store.

recent_posts.title: Open source inference engine for small models in AI search and agentic workflows
recent_posts.summary: Superlinked's Filip Makraduli presents the open-source Superlinked Inference Engine (SIE), built to fill a gap in small model inference infrastructure for AI search and document processing. The talk covers why small models matter for agentic workflows (context rot management, tool calling, preprocessing), what inference is not (just adding GPUs), and the 'yin and yang' approach combining broad model support with production-grade infrastructure. Key technical highlights include hot-swapping multiple small models on a single GPU with LRU eviction, re-implementing forward passes to handle architectural differences across BERT, Qwen, and ColBERT, variable-length flash attention for efficient token batching, and a full infrastructure stack with KEDA autoscaling, Prometheus metrics, Helm charts, and Terraform-based GPU provisioning. The engine has been tested with Chroma, Qdrant, Weaviate, and LanceDB.

recent_posts.title: Accelerating AI on Edge — Chintan Parikh and Weiyi Wang, Google DeepMind
recent_posts.summary: Google DeepMind's Chintan Parikh presents the Gemma 4 edge models (2B and 4B parameter variants) and the LiteRT on-device inference framework. Key topics include benefits of edge AI deployment (latency, privacy, cost), new Gemma 4 capabilities like function calling, structured JSON output, and chain-of-thought reasoning, plus a demo gallery app showcasing on-device agent skills. The LiteRT framework supports cross-platform deployment across Android, iOS, macOS, Linux, Windows, Raspberry Pi, and IoT devices, with NPU acceleration from Qualcomm and MediaTek delivering up to 13x performance boosts. Models are available on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0 and support PyTorch and JAX conversion paths.

recent_posts.title: Demand-driven context approach for improving AI agent performance in enterprises
recent_posts.summary: A staff software engineer at IKEA presents a 'demand-driven context' approach to solving the institutional knowledge gap that prevents AI agents from delivering real enterprise value. Rather than pushing all documentation to agents via RAG or MCP servers, the approach lets agents pull context by failing on real work items (Jira tickets, incidents) and explicitly requesting what they need. This surfaces undocumented tribal knowledge, curates it into structured context blocks, and gradually improves agent autonomy. A context gap scanner tool automates the process at scale by running past incidents against the knowledge base to identify missing, stale, or duplicated documentation and prioritize fixes via a Kanban-style board.
